judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: Plain and breathless like Nox, but the two outcomes are near-twins built on the same 'token of my gratitude/appreciation' stock phrase, and trolls carrying off students and a hat is a pile-up of invented colour with no Nox-specific mechanics.

items.label: B
items.critique: The second ask ('You, again. Will you think it over, buy me an ale...') doesn't follow from the first, and the refusal line is clumsy. The quest crams in a lead to the next step ('maybe you can find a way in') in a way Westwood's short speeches rarely do.

items.label: C
items.critique: Very plain and short with the '20 in gold' price idiom and a dry joke ('Since I like your face'), all of which fits Nox. It's a near guess, but the neat fee-plus-vendor pairing feels built to order.

items.label: D
items.critique: Sponsorship petition, an urchin that has stirred up the bats, and a ruby key for the orchard gate: concrete, functional and slightly absurd, in plain uneven sentences. It reads like a real level hook.

items.label: E
items.critique: The shop line is fine, but the chain-yanking favour comes with no stated purpose or reward, and the 'It roared! ... You're my lucky charm!' payoff is humour reaching for whimsy instead of Nox's deadpan.

items.label: F
items.critique: A full bounty arc with a surrender line, a constable who heard the racket, and alive-versus-dead rewards (200/100 in gold). It has Nox's exclamatory, plain register and lets the quest's mechanics show in the dialogue.

items.label: G
items.critique: The grumbling smuggler ('Sometimes I think he does this just to get away from his responsibilities'), the jailbreak and the warning about the wizards' tower have Westwood's light comic plainness and clear reward lines.

items.label: H
items.critique: An absurd 50,000-gold offer to buy an inn, delivered deadpan with 'lad'. This is the kind of throwaway joke Westwood put in its towns.

items.label: I
items.critique: The apprentice fee, the spellbook and a field guide that lets you charm spiders all tie straight to game mechanics, with a casual 'Ya want one?'. It reads as authentic tutorial-style Nox text.

items.label: J
items.critique: A near-copy of F's opener with the nouns swapped (ore carts, claim-jumpers, gallows), and its second ask echoes H's 'Actually, business has fallen off'. It also leaks an unmasked invented name ('Snade').

tells: Generated texts reuse stock phrases from other texts in the set ('token of my gratitude', 'Actually, business/trade has...', 'I presume you've come about the notice') with only the nouns swapped.

Westwood's asks tie straight to game mechanics (keys, field guides, spells, sponsorship petitions, prices in gold), while generated ones lean on invented local colour (hats, ale, furnace chains) with vaguer stakes.
Generated pairs of asks and outcomes are often near-symmetrical or don't connect (an outcome that doesn't answer its ask, or a second ask that doesn't follow from the first).
Westwood's humour is deadpan and situational (a 50,000-gold inn, a smuggler who gets arrested on purpose). Generated humour is more exclaimed and whimsical ('It roared!', 'lucky charm').
Generated outcomes tend to add a forward-pointing lead to the next quest step in one long speech; Westwood keeps thanks short and to the reward.
